content: The international conventions governing the trade of pesticides impose specific obligations on participating countries. Additionally, countries exporting banned or severely restricted chemicals must provide an export notification to the importing country. The Rotterdam Convention is a key legally binding framework for international pesticide trade, but the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants also regulates the import and export of pesticides listed in its Annexes A and B. These pesticides can only be imported or exported for environmentally sound disposal or for permitted uses approved by the importing country under specific exemptions. The Prior Informed Consent (PIC) procedure under the Rotterdam Convention is a formal mechanism to obtain and disseminate decisions from importing countries on whether they will accept future shipments of chemicals listed in Annex III. Exporting countries are required to comply with these decisions. Import decisions must be trade-neutral, meaning that if a country refuses to import a specific chemical, it must also cease domestic production of that chemical for local use and reject imports from all sources, including non-member countries. The Basel Convention allows countries to prohibit the import or export of hazardous wastes or specific types of hazardous waste shipments. This requires countries to manage stocks of obsolete pesticide products effectively. Exporting countries may only transport hazardous wastes across borders after providing prior written notification to the importing and transit countries and receiving their written consent. Pesticide laws typically require all individuals or businesses involved in manufacturing, importing, formulating, packaging, repackaging, distributing, or selling pesticides to hold a valid license. This license is a formal written authorization issued for a specific period by the responsible authority. Pest control operators (PCOs), aerial applicators, and other specialized applicators are also generally required to obtain licenses. Countries with severe restrictions on certain pesticides often mandate special licenses for their use. Authorities can periodically verify that licensed operators meet legal requirements and possess the necessary training, resources, and capacity to handle pesticides safely. Licensing differs from registration. While registration evaluates the product and its associated risks, licensing assesses the suitability of individuals or entities to handle already-registered pesticides. Licensing requirements may include appropriate storage facilities, record-keeping, and basic knowledge of pesticides. Licensing systems may also encourage the use of lower-risk pesticides by imposing stricter requirements or higher fees for higher-risk products. Applications for licenses must follow specified procedures, and authorities are empowered to charge fees, set license validity terms, and establish renewal or transfer processes. Authorities can suspend or revoke licenses if inspections reveal non-compliance, violations of license conditions, or new information that would have led to the denial of the original application. Applicants denied a license or whose license is suspended or revoked must be provided with written reasons and an opportunity to appeal. Licensing requirements may vary by country and are often adapted to local regulatory needs. National inspection and enforcement capacities must be considered when establishing licensing schemes. In decentralized systems, local or provincial authorities may implement central-level legislation and their own provisions. The type and quality of products are often regulated under pesticide legislation, while site selection, environmental safety, and worker health are governed by other laws. Licensing for manufacturing must also reflect international obligations, such as those under the Rotterdam Convention, which requires countries to prohibit domestic production of chemicals they refuse to import. Efficient record-keeping and communication systems are critical to prevent the approval of chemicals rejected under the PIC procedure for domestic production or use. Pesticide legislation must regulate packaging and repackaging to prevent risks to human health and the environment. Packaging must be safe for storage, handling, and use, and should not resemble containers for consumable goods. Repackaging should only occur on licensed premises with adequate protections against toxic hazards. Governments should prohibit repackaging pesticides into food or drink containers and may require permits for repackaging. Exceptions may be made for emergency repackaging of damaged containers to prevent contamination, provided the new containers are properly labeled. Labels should be in the national language(s) and include internationally recognized symbols, pictograms, and color codes. Legislation should specify the information required on labels, such as product content, hazard and safety information, directions for use, and supplier identification. Labels must be affixed to the smallest saleable unit and include essential information even if additional details are provided in an accompanying leaflet. Labels should be resistant to damage and degradation under normal storage and use conditions. Following international guidelines, such as the FAO/WHO Guidelines on Good Labeling Practice for Pesticides, promotes harmonization of labeling standards globally.
